Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. For every beat, provide one distinct complete factual claim, a concrete example, a concise editable visual direction, and one or two exact supplied source IDs. End the claim, example, and visual direction with complete punctuation. Every cited source excerpt must directly support the claim; reuse at least two important technical terms from each cited excerpt so support can be checked locally. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Keep the claim, example, and visual direction compact; a deterministic local expander will produce the full narration. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Every factual claim must cite one or more supplied source IDs. Narration must describe information that is essential to understand visuals. Do not imitate a named creator or invent sources.
input.prompt:
Topic: CSCI-462: Introduction to Cryptography. Create a representative course-foundations companion aligned to the official catalog description. It must teach durable concepts and problem-solving methods without claiming to replace the instructor's syllabus. Official catalog description: This course provides an introduction to cryptography, its mathematical foundations, and its relation to security. It covers classical cryptosystems, private-key cryptosystems (including DES and AES), hashing and public-key cryptosystems (including RSA). The course also provides an introduction to data integrity and authentication. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-662. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or CSEC-202) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

Source excerpts:

[nist-cryptographic-standards]
Cryptographic standards define approved algorithms and parameters. Encryption supports confidentiality when keys and modes are used correctly. Message authentication and digital signatures address integrity and authenticity in different ways. Random number generation supports keys, nonces, and other security parameters. Key management covers generation, distribution, storage, use, rotation, revocation, and destruction. Modes of operation define how a primitive processes data larger than one block. Validation checks implementations against specified requirements. Security depends on the complete protocol and implementation, not only an algorithm name. Analysis also considers side channels and migration requirements.

[nist-ssdf]
The Secure Software Development Framework groups practices into four practice groups. Prepare the Organization establishes people, processes, and technology for secure development. Protect the Software prevents unauthorized access to code and development artifacts. Produce Well-Secured Software addresses security requirements, design, verification, and release. Respond to Vulnerabilities identifies, analyzes, remediates, and learns from discovered weaknesses. Security requirements should be tracked throughout development. Verification provides evidence that selected practices and controls were performed. Security reasoning identifies assets, trust boundaries, threats, controls, evidence, residual risk, and responsibilities.

[rit-csci-462]
This course provides an introduction to cryptography, its mathematical foundations, and its relation to security. It covers classical cryptosystems, private-key cryptosystems (including DES and AES), hashing and public-key cryptosystems (including RSA). The course also provides an introduction to data integrity and authentication. Students cannot take and receive credit for this course if they have credit for CSCI-662. Prerequisites: (CSCI-243 or SWEN-262 or CSEC-202) and (MATH-190 or MATH-200) or equivalent courses. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring, Summer

beats.claim: Cryptography relies on mathematical foundations and standardized algorithms to protect data confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
beats.example: AES encryption uses a symmetric key to transform plaintext into ciphertext, ensuring only authorized parties can read the message.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Foundations of Cryptographic Systems
beats.visualDirection: Display a side-by-side comparison of plaintext and ciphertext with a symmetric key lock icon, labeled 'Confidentiality via AES'.

beats.claim: Classical cryptosystems like substitution and transposition ciphers form the historical basis for modern encryption techniques.
beats.example: The Caesar cipher shifts each letter by a fixed number, demonstrating how simple substitution can be broken with frequency analysis.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Classical Cryptosystems Overview
beats.visualDirection: Show a Caesar cipher alphabet wheel with 'A' shifting to 'D', annotated with 'Substitution Vulnerability'.

beats.claim: Private-key cryptosystems use a single shared secret key for both encryption and decryption, enabling efficient symmetric encryption.
beats.example: DES and AES require the same key for encrypting and decrypting data, making them fast but dependent on secure key distribution.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Private-Key Cryptosystems
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a two-way arrow between 'Sender' and 'Receiver' with a single key symbol, labeled 'Symmetric Key Exchange'.

beats.claim: Public-key cryptosystems use a mathematically linked key pair, allowing secure communication without prior key exchange.
beats.example: RSA uses a public key for encryption and a private key for decryption, solving the key distribution problem in symmetric systems.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Public-Key Cryptosystems
beats.visualDirection: Draw a split key icon: 'Public Key' (open hand) and 'Private Key' (closed fist), labeled 'Asymmetric Key Pair'.

beats.claim: Hashing algorithms produce fixed-size outputs from variable-size inputs, enabling data integrity verification and collision resistance.
beats.example: SHA-256 generates a unique 256-bit hash for a document, where altering any bit changes the entire output.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Hashing Functions
beats.visualDirection: Show a document entering a hash function box, outputting a long hex string, labeled 'Integrity Check via SHA-256'.

beats.claim: Message authentication and digital signatures ensure data has not been tampered with and verify the sender's identity.
beats.example: A digital signature uses the sender's private key to sign a message, which the receiver verifies with the public key.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Data Integrity and Authentication
beats.visualDirection: Display a document with a signature stamp and a verification checkmark, labeled 'Authenticity via Digital Signatures'.

beats.claim: Secure key management covers generation, distribution, storage, rotation, and destruction to prevent unauthorized access.
beats.example: Keys must be stored in hardware security modules and rotated regularly to limit exposure if compromised.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Key Management Practices
beats.visualDirection: Show a key lifecycle diagram: 'Generate' -> 'Store' -> 'Use' -> 'Rotate' -> 'Destroy', with lock icons at each stage.

beats.claim: Modes of operation define how block ciphers process data larger than one block, enabling efficient encryption of arbitrary-length messages.
beats.example: CBC mode uses a chaining value to link blocks, preventing pattern repetition in encrypted output.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Modes of Operation
beats.visualDirection: Illustrate a block cipher processing two blocks with a feedback loop, labeled 'CBC Mode Chaining'.

beats.claim: Security depends on complete protocol design and implementation validation, not just algorithm selection, to prevent side-channel attacks.
beats.example: Timing attacks can exploit variable execution times in cryptographic libraries, requiring constant-time implementations for validation.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Security Implementation & Validation
beats.visualDirection: Show a security checklist with items: 'Algorithm Validated', 'Implementation Tested', 'Side-Channel Mitigated', labeled 'Validation Checklist'.

beats.claim: Students must evaluate cryptographic systems by checking key management, algorithm standards, integrity mechanisms, and implementation security.
beats.example: A secure system uses AES for confidentiality, SHA-256 for integrity, RSA for authentication, and follows NIST key management standards.
beats.title: Lesson Title: Practical Analysis Checklist
beats.visualDirection: Display a practical analysis checklist with checkboxes: 'Confidentiality Mechanism', 'Integrity Check', 'Authentication Method', 'Key Management', 'Implementation Validated'.

learningObjectives: Define the core components of cryptographic systems, including confidentiality, integrity, and authentication.
Explain how mathematical foundations and standardized algorithms enable secure data protection.
Apply cryptographic principles to evaluate real-world security implementations and identify common vulnerabilities.
